points.why: It treats absenteeism as several problems under one label, with each stakeholder seeing a real piece, but it never says the definition itself is contested or that a plan built on one group's framing will be resisted by the others.

It asks each group what evidence would change their mind and proposes interviewing students and families, but it hands diagnosis to a neutral analyst rather than building a shared picture with all stakeholders together.
It describes how the causes feed each other and sets out a test for each claim, but it doesn't question the beliefs, ownership or who-acts assumptions behind each group's preferred fix.
It doesn't track which groups have been consulted or informed, and it moves to data analysis on every claim without first getting agreement on definitions.

pitfalls.why: It explicitly rejects picking and funding a single most likely cause.

notes: It claims the disagreement exists only because no one has checked the data, which treats a partly value-based dispute (e.g. whose job attendance is) as purely empirical.
